issues.item: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategies are not well anchored to the reported trauma type of childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. Avoiding hospitals/ambulances/physical examinations suggests a medical-trauma theme, while avoiding public transport and enclosed spaces suggests transport or confinement-related trauma. Those themes are not supported by the trigger or threat items, which instead center on interpersonal conflict, crying, and hypervigilant safety positioning.

issues.item: Avoid Public Transport: Using public transport
issues.explanation: Within the strategy node, the three avoidance items point to three different situational themes—medical settings, transport, and enclosed spaces—without corresponding support from memory, appraisal, or trigger content. This makes the strategy profile look internally diffuse rather than like a coherent set of coping responses for one trauma formulation.

issues.item: Triggers: Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event
issues.explanation: The profile is only partially coherent for childhood physical abuse. Arguments, crying, and conflict avoidance fit the trauma type, but the combination of a highly specific tactile-texture trigger with public transport avoidance and enclosed-space avoidance is difficult to link to this trauma history without any memory or appraisal content explaining that association.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Public Transport: Using public transport
issues.explanation: Within the threat/strategy pattern, back-to-wall positioning and safe-seat seeking imply marked hypervigilance in public or interpersonal environments, which could plausibly connect to transport avoidance, but enclosed-space avoidance suggests a more circumscribed claustrophobic or situational fear that is not otherwise represented in the trigger set.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Enclosed Spaces: Enclosed or confined spaces
issues.explanation: Given the formulation, Threat and Maladaptive Strategies are tightly linked, and Maladaptive Strategies strongly feed Triggers. Avoiding conflict fits the trigger set (arguments, crying), but avoiding public transport and enclosed spaces target contexts not reflected by the listed triggers, making the node contents insufficiently aligned with the edge pattern.

issues.item: Avoid Public Transport: Using public transport
issues.explanation: Avoiding public transport is not well supported by the rest of the profile for childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. The listed triggers are arguments, crying, and unexpected touch, and the threat items center on interpersonal vigilance and positioning in rooms. Public transport avoidance suggests a different trigger/threat context and is hard to link coherently to the other selected items.

issues.item: Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building
issues.explanation: Avoiding being alone is not clearly connected to the rest of the profile. The threat items describe hypervigilance in shared spaces and interpersonal danger cues, while the triggers are interpersonal/emotional and tactile. Being alone as a primary avoidance target pulls toward a different clinical pattern unless there were accompanying abandonment or panic-related items, which are absent here.

Difficulty concentrating is a nonspecific PTSD symptom rather than a threat appraisal/perceived current danger item. Within this node, the other threat items specifically reflect situational safety behaviors and surveillance of the environment. This item does not fit the node's theme and weakens alignment with the formulation in which Threat is tightly linked to Maladaptive Strategies.

vignette:
Amir is a nineteen-year-old environmental scientist who was physically abused by his father throughout his childhood. He cannot remember a time before the beatings, only the sharp, unpredictable escalation-a raised voice, a slammed hand on a table-that would precede a blow. He learned to read the subtle shifts in his father's face: the tightening of the jaw, the narrowing of the eyes, the slight tilt of the head that meant he was about to be struck. That hypervigilance never left him. Now, as an adult, he scans every room he enters for an exit, and he always chooses a seat with his back to a wall. He studies the faces and body language of everyone around him, searching for the same warning signs he once relied on to survive.

Amir works in a small field laboratory with a team of five. The work is precise and collaborative, and disagreements are common-about sampling protocols, data interpretation, shift schedules. For Amir, every argument feels like the first step toward violence. When a colleague raises their voice in frustration, his heart pounds and his vision narrows. He begins to scan their face for the familiar signs of impending attack. The raised voice itself becomes a trigger, but so do the crying of a coworker after a difficult call, or the unexpected touch of a hand on his shoulder when he is bent over a microscope. Each of these moments activates the same threat system he developed as a child.

In response, Amir has developed a set of strategies that he believes keep him safe. He avoids any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation, even when his professional opinion is needed. He agrees to protocols he knows are flawed rather than risk a debate. He avoids being alone in the lab or his apartment, because when he is alone, his mind replays the old scenes, and the threat feels closer. Most of all, he avoids other people. He has stopped joining his team for lunch, and he leaves the lab as soon as his shift ends, walking home quickly with his head down, scanning the street for anyone who might approach him.

These strategies, however, have a paradoxical effect. By avoiding people, he has fewer opportunities to test his predictions about safety, so his belief that others are dangerous remains unchallenged. More concretely, his colleagues have noticed his withdrawal. When he avoids a team meeting, they talk about his absence, and one of them-frustrated by his silence on a project-raises her voice at him the next day. That argument, in turn, becomes a new trigger, reinforcing his sense that confrontation is dangerous. His avoidance creates the very conditions that produce the triggers he fears.

The most dominant loop in Amir's life is this: a trigger-a raised voice, a crying coworker, an unexpected touch-activates his threat system. He scans faces, positions himself with his back to a wall, and feels unsafe until he can control his environment. This threat state then drives him to avoid the people and situations that might produce the trigger again. But his avoidance, by isolating him and creating social friction, makes it more likely that someone will confront him or express frustration, which becomes a new trigger. The cycle tightens around him. He has come to believe that he cannot trust anyone, that safety is a temporary condition he must constantly manage, and that any moment of relaxation will be punished.

What finally brought Amir to seek help was a moment at work two weeks ago. A senior scientist, unaware of Amir's history, placed a hand on his shoulder to congratulate him on a successful analysis. Amir reacted by flinching violently, knocking over a tray of samples. The silence in the lab afterward was unbearable. He went home that night and told his wife he could not keep living this way. He is most afraid that therapy will ask him to stop avoiding-that he will have to sit with the threat, to let people touch him, to endure arguments without fleeing. But he is also afraid of what will happen if he does not change. He is hoping, quietly, that someone can teach him a different way to read a face.
